move: Affirms that the Just/Expedient distinction is real and the most sacred part of morality while denying any standard of justice not grounded on utility, so justice is neither imaginary nor independently real.

Reduces justice to those moral requirements highest in social utility, admits other duties can override them, and treats its apparent indefeasibility as preserved only by a useful accommodation of language.

Analyses the idea of justice by locating the mark of duty in the thought that performance may rightfully be exacted, distinguishing morality from expediency without settling whether justice is objective.
Casts justice and injustice as health and disease of the soul, making justice the institution of a natural order and government among the soul's parts rather than an agreed arrangement.
Displays the unresolved conflict between retributive and deterrent tests of just punishment as evidence that the sentiment of justice delivers no single determinate standard.
Notes that justice reaches beyond what law does or should regulate yet still carries the lingering idea of what ought to be law, describing the concept's scope rather than adjudicating its status.
Finds one and the same form of justice in state and individual — each part doing its own business — and treats it as a primary form discovered, and divinely led to, rather than instituted.
Demarcates justice from other morality by aligning it with duties of perfect obligation, which have a correlative personal right, an analytic distinction that takes no side on objectivity.

Argues that if justice were an independent standard per se known by introspection its internal oracle would not be so ambiguous, since disagreement about the just is as fierce as about the useful, even within one mind.
Separates the origin of the feeling of justice from its binding force and poses as still open whether the reality behind it is intrinsically peculiar or merely a combination of other qualities.
Debunks the maxim volenti non fit injuria as an instructive specimen of the loose and irregular way supposed principles of justice grow up, arising from the coarse exigencies of courts.

Derives equality and impartiality as the highest abstract standard of distributive justice toward which all institutions should converge, resting it on a deeper foundation that emanates directly from the first principle of morals.
